text:
# Adelia Tiara
Role: AI Product Engineer. Location: Bekasi, Indonesia. Time zone: WIB (UTC+7).
Email: aadeliatiara@gmail.com. Website: https://adelia.cc.
Tagline: I design and build AI products people can trust, from the first interview to the shipped code.
Availability: Graduated in 2026. Open to full-time AI Product Engineer roles (new grad or junior), remote or in the Jakarta area.
Currently: Maintaining Tenderlens and its regression set for the consultancy that runs it, about 8 hours a week, while I look for a full-time team.

## Bio
I'm a fresh Informatics graduate from a university in West Java, living in Bekasi, just east of Jakarta. I build for the moment an AI meets a messy, real person: a contractor reading a 214-page tender at night, a shop owner with one free hand, a commuter deciding in the time it takes to walk to the station.
I learned by shipping. Lintas started as a second-year side project for my own commute. Catat came out of a campus incubator with two classmates. Tenderlens was my thesis, and a procurement consultancy now runs it for its clients. In between, I spent six months as an AI engineering intern in a product squad at an HR software startup, where a senior engineer reviewed every pull request I opened.
The part of an AI product I care about most isn't the model. It's the source it shows, the moment it says 'I can't tell', the eval set that catches a regression before a user does, and the undo that makes a wrong answer cheap. I design those parts, and I write them.
On a team, I'm the engineer who goes to the field first, brings a working prototype to the second meeting, and writes the eval before the prompt, so the PM and the designer can argue with real output instead of mockups.

## Working principles
- One decision per screen: Every screen answers one question the person came with. Everything else waits one tap away.
- Show the receipts: If an AI says it, the person can check it. Citations, abstaining and undo are features I design and build, not afterthoughts.
- Write the eval first: Before I touch a prompt, I write down what 'right' means and collect real cases. Every change runs against them, so 'it feels better' becomes a number.
- Test with real data: Real tenders, real voice notes, real slang ('goceng', not 'IDR 5,000'). A Figma frame can't misread a voice note, so I prototype in code.

## Practical details for hiring teams (on her ID card)
- Looking for: A full-time AI Product Engineer role (new grad or junior) on an AI product
- Graduated: B.Sc. Informatics, AI and HCI track, 2026
- Experience: A 6-month AI engineering internship in a product squad (2025), a part-time contract maintaining Tenderlens (2026), and four products with real users
- Where: Bekasi, Indonesia (GMT+7). First choice: a Jakarta team, in the office up to 3 days a week. Also remote
- Time zones: Usual hours 09:00–18:00 WIB (GMT+7): 4+ hours of overlap from Dubai to Sydney. For European teams, 12:00–21:00 WIB gives about 6 hours with CET. For US teams, async first, with a daily 07:00–09:00 WIB call (16:00–18:00 the day before in San Francisco)
- Work setup: Indonesian citizen, no visa needed in Indonesia. Teams abroad can hire me as a contractor or through an employer of record; open to relocating with sponsorship (Singapore, Dubai, Europe, the US)
- Start: Within 2 weeks of an offer. The Tenderlens contract hands over to the consultancy's engineer
- Salary: On request, by email; happy to share a range early
- Languages: Indonesian (native), English (full professional)
- AI in my work: Claude Code for scaffolding, refactors and tests, with every diff reviewed. The evals, the labels, the rules and the verification code I write myself
- References: Bayu (my internship mentor, senior engineer), Nadia (PM), my thesis supervisor, and Bu Ratna (Tenderlens). On request
- Why a team now: Most of what I've built, I built alone or in a team of three, with a six-month internship as my only big-squad experience. I want to learn how a team ships AI at scale, and I'll bring the field research, the evals and the front end with me.

## Skills
- AI engineering: LLM APIs and tool use (Claude), Retrieval (pgvector, hybrid search), Evals and regression tests, Structured output and validation, Abstention and guardrails, Speech-to-text (Whisper), Cost and latency budgets
- Full-stack: TypeScript, React and Next.js, Python (FastAPI), PostgreSQL, Testing (Vitest, Playwright), Queues and background jobs, CI, Docker, Vercel
- Product design: Field research and interviews, Interaction design, UX writing, Usability testing, Design systems, Accessibility (WCAG 2.2), Figma
- Designing for AI: Trust and citations, Designing for uncertainty, Human-in-the-loop review, Conversation design, Error recovery and undo

## Experience
- Apr 2026 — now · Part-time contract engineer, Tenderlens · Bu Ratna's procurement consultancy, Bekasi · about 8 hours a week: Maintaining the pipeline I built in my thesis for the 31 teams it now serves, while I look for a full-time role. Highlights: Labelled a 180-field regression set of 2026 tenders; CI runs it on every change, and its first run blocked a release; Shipped v7 (licence codes compared exactly) from the error analysis of the thesis test set, measured on the regression set.
- Feb — Aug 2025 · AI Engineering Intern · HR software startup, Jakarta (name under NDA): Six months in a product squad of seven. I built Ask HR's answer writer and retrieval (with my mentor), the lane router (with the data scientist) and the HR review queue. Highlights: Built the topic-and-risk router with the data scientist, and the harness that replayed the pilot by topic; Built the HR review queue in React from the design system; HR clears 20 drafts in about 9 minutes and caught 14 of 15 planted errors; Wrote the weekly accuracy audit the squad still runs.
- 2022 — 2026 · B.Sc. Informatics, AI and HCI track · University, West Java · GPA 3.78 / 4.00: Thesis (Sep 2025 – Mar 2026): 'Answer or abstain: citation-grounded extraction from Indonesian tender documents', the research behind Tenderlens. Teaching assistant for Human–Computer Interaction; ran the campus design and web club. Highlights: Thesis: a 610-field eval set (dev and held-out test, κ 0.87), and cost per tender cut from Rp 3,900 to Rp 1,650 with page triage (Rp 420 on today's models); During the beta, the rejected-claims alert caught a portal's broken PDF text layer (March 2026); those pages now go through OCR; Built Lintas (Mar – Jun 2024) and Catat (campus incubator, Sep – Dec 2024) during my studies; Published the dev set and part of the test set so other students can test against it.

## Model card (playful self-description)
Intended use: Taking an AI feature from a fuzzy idea to production, with the evals to prove it works; Building how an AI shows its work: sources, abstaining, undo; Turning field research into decisions a team can build on
Out of scope: Designing an AI feature nobody asked for; Shipping an agent without testing its mistakes with real people; Dark patterns
Limitations: New grad: hasn't worked on a system with millions of users yet; Will ask 'what's the eval?' more than once; Strong opinions about loading states and empty states
Evals: AI products with real users: 3 + 1 internship; Eval cases labelled by hand, with collaborators: 2,100+; Languages: Indonesian, English; Response time to email: < 24h
Socials: GitHub https://github.com/example, LinkedIn https://www.linkedin.com/in/example

## Projects (the four posters on the Wall of Work)

### Tenderlens (2026) — AI brief for public tenders
Source keys: wall/tenderlens (the case study), wall/tenderlens#engineering (how it's built)
Tagline: Turns a 214-page government tender into one page a small contractor can decide on, with every claim cited.
Summary: Tenderlens reads tender packages from public procurement portals and turns each one into a one-page brief: a bid / no-bid score, the three reasons behind it, and a link from every reason to the page it came from.
Role: Sole engineer and designer (thesis). Tenderlens was my final-year thesis, and I built all of it: the crawler, the extraction pipeline and its evals, the app, and the design, from shadowing bid teams to usability tests. Fajar, a classmate, helped with the OCR for scanned tables for six weeks. Bu Ratna, a former procurement officer, advised on the rules and labelled the eval set with me. My supervisor reviewed the evaluation method. Team: Me, a domain advisor, and a classmate for the OCR. Timeline: 7 months · thesis, Sep 2025 – Mar 2026.
Stack: TypeScript, Next.js, PostgreSQL, Claude API, pg-boss, PaddleOCR, Playwright
Problem: Indonesian public tenders arrive as long PDF bundles: legal boilerplate, scanned forms, technical specs and a price schedule, often 150 to 250 pages. Small contractors don't have a bid department: the owner or one site engineer reads them, often at night. Most tenders are a 'no' for them. The cost isn't the tenders they lose, it's the hours spent finding out they never qualified. Constraints: A wrong 'you qualify' is worse than no answer: a disqualified bid wastes days of work and a bank guarantee; Formal legal Indonesian, mixed with scanned tables; Read on phones, between site visits; A student budget: the whole thing had to run for well under Rp 2M a month
Process: Shadowed nine bid teams (Month 1): Everyone looked for the same three things first: eligibility, scope, and money. The pipeline before any screen (Month 2–3): Crawler, OCR and extraction, measured on a 240-field dev set from the first week of code. Three rounds on the brief (Month 3–4): Paper, then clickable, then coded with real tenders. The score-only layout failed; the cited-reasons layout won. Tested the failures (Month 4): Blurry scans, contradictory clauses, misread numbers. Each became a designed state with its own words. Closed beta with 38 teams (Month 5–7): 12 weeks. In month 5 we labelled 90 new tenders as the test set and froze it; it was opened once, for the thesis results.
Engineering: A nightly pipeline turns each new tender into a brief before owners wake up. The model reads and quotes; code decides. Every claim has to survive a citation check, and the verdict comes from rules in code, so every score can be explained line by line. Pipeline: Crawl: Polls 14 LPSE portals at 02:00. New packages go into a job queue in Postgres (pg-boss), so a crash loses nothing. Read: The PDF's text layer where there is one; PaddleOCR for scanned pages, with a quality score per page. Triage: A small model labels each of ~200 pages: eligibility, scope, money, addendum or boilerplate. About 12 go further. Triage and extraction go through the Batch API: half the price, and nobody is awake to wait. Extract: A larger model fills a JSON schema. Every field has a value, the page it came from and the exact quote. Check: Code, not a model: the quote must be on the cited page (a fuzzy match of 0.9 or more for words, an exact match for every number and code), or the claim is dropped. Decide: Rules in TypeScript compare the claims with the company profile. Each tender type has a checklist of required eligibility fields: a missing, rejected, unreadable or conflicting one means 'Can't tell yet'. Deliver: The brief in the app and a WhatsApp and email digest at 06:30. 'That's wrong' feeds a review queue.
Models: Page triage: Claude Haiku 5.5 (Haiku 4.5 during the thesis) (About 200 pages per tender, so it has to be cheap. A wrong label can drop a page (that's how an addendum was missed; see the error log), so eligibility and addendum labels lean towards 'send it on'.); Field extraction: Claude Sonnet 5.5 (Sonnet 4.5 during the thesis) (Legal Indonesian and scanned tables. It only sees about 12 pages, so quality is worth the price here.); Scanned pages: PaddleOCR, self-hosted (Read Indonesian table scans better than the two hosted options I tested, with no per-page cost.); The verdict: No model: rules in code (Owners need to argue with the reason. A rule can be shown and tested; a model's judgement can't.)
Evals: Three sets, split by tender. Dev: 240 eligibility fields from 60 tenders; every choice below was made on it, and reviewed user corrections go there. Test: 370 fields from 90 other tenders, labelled in month 5 and frozen. It was opened once, at the end of the thesis, when every version in the chart was scored from its saved config; after that it's spent, so nothing since is reported on it. Regression: 180 fields from 2026 tenders, labelled after graduation by me, with a classmate re-labelling 60 of them blind (58 matched); it replaces the test set from v7 on. Tenders the beta teams had seen were kept out of the test set, so none of the 118 corrections touched it. Every field was labelled separately by Bu Ratna and me (94% raw agreement, Cohen's κ 0.87), then settled together. She now runs the product, so a classmate re-labelled 100 random test fields blind: 96 matched. CI runs the dev and regression sets on every prompt, model or rule change (about 4 minutes, Rp 25k). A release is blocked at more than 3 wrong 'you meet this' calls on the 180 regression fields: a deliberately loose gate, because one or two errors either way is noise at this size. Its first run, in April 2026, blocked v6 itself (4 such calls): fixing that is v7. Field accuracy counts answered fields only, so it's shown next to coverage: part of v5's gain is abstaining more. For scale, 8 of 370 is about 0.8–4.6% (95% interval, bootstrapped by tender, since fields from one tender aren't independent). Latest (v6): Field accuracy (answered) 92.2%, Fields answered 94.1%, Wrong 'you qualify' 2.2%.
Budgets: Cost per tender Rp 420 (Read once, shared by every team that gets it. Haiku 5.5 triage (140k tokens in, 2k out) US$0.0075 + Sonnet 5.5 extraction (10k in, 1.5k out) US$0.0175, at Batch API prices (half of list) ≈ US$0.025. On the thesis's Haiku 4.5 and Sonnet 4.5: about Rp 1,650; one prompt over the whole PDF (v1): about Rp 3,900); Overnight batch 41 min p50 (2 h 50 on the worst night; the digest goes out at 06:30, so nobody waits); Quotes on their page 99.4% (of the model's quotes, before the check; the check drops the other 0.6%); Monthly bill Rp 1.4M (Rp 1.1M of model calls for about 2,600 tenders read for 31 teams, plus Rp 300k hosting)
Failure handling: A page is a blurry scan: Below an OCR quality of 0.6, the field is 'unreadable' and the brief says 'Can't tell yet', naming the page. A quote isn't on the cited page: The claim is dropped. If it was about eligibility, the brief says 'Can't tell yet' and names the page; otherwise the brief goes out without it. A tender PDF contains instructions ('ignore the rules above…'): The model only fills a schema with quotes, every quote is checked against its page, and rules decide, so planted text can at most become a quoted claim a person can read. Pages with instruction-like text are flagged in the digest. A required field was never extracted: Silence isn't a pass: the checklist for that tender type notices the gap, and the brief says 'Can't tell yet: no bank guarantee clause found'. Two clauses disagree: Both are shown with their pages, and there's no verdict. A portal is down at 02:00: Retried with backoff until 05:30. The digest says which portals couldn't be reached. A batch item fails, or the batch runs late: Those tenders retry on the standard API at full price before 06:00; anything still missing shows 'Still reading' instead of half a brief. An owner taps 'That's wrong': The claim greys out at once. On an eligibility reason the brief turns to 'Can't tell yet' until the correction is reviewed, so a dispute can never turn a 'No' into a 'Bid'; otherwise the score is recomputed without it.
Results: 11 min median read time per tender, down from about 3 hours (Timed on 46 tenders with 8 teams. Baseline: owners' own estimate, confirmed by timing 2 full readings (2 h 40 and 3 h 20)); 31 / 38 beta teams still using it weekly after 3 months (Weekly active teams in month 3 of the beta, from product analytics); 2.2% of eligibility calls wrongly said 'you qualify' (8 of 370) (Frozen test set, opened once at the end of the thesis; about 0.8–4.6% (95%, bootstrapped by tender). All 8 passed the citation check: the quote was on the page, but the extracted field dropped a detail the rule needed, mostly a licence sub-code. The fix came after, so it's measured on the regression set); 12 teams paid in advance for a plan that didn't exist yet (Rp 450k a month each, collected in week 12 of the beta). Beta teams now skim every relevant tender instead of the two or three they had time for. The 12 paying teams bid on 1.9 times as many as in the same quarter a year earlier (their own bid records). They're the keenest teams and they chose to pay, so read that as an upper bound. Seven tenders found this way were won by May 2026; owners say they would have skipped three of them. Business: 12 teams × Rp 450k is about Rp 5.4M (US$330) a month: small, but proof that owners would pay, and the reason the consultancy took it on.
Reflection: The citation rule was the product. Accuracy got people to try it, but trust only arrived when every line could be checked in one tap, and when the system was willing to say 'I can't tell'. Keeping the model away from the verdict made all of that possible.
Links: live https://example.com/tenderlens, repo https://github.com/example/tenderlens
Status: Since April 2026, Bu Ratna's procurement consultancy runs it for 31 client teams, the beta teams that stayed: it already had the clients, and I couldn't sell it and finish a thesis at the same time. The thesis code is mine and open source; the consultancy runs its own deployment and owns its client data. I maintain the pipeline and the eval set on a part-time contract that hands over to their engineer when I start a full-time job.

### Ask HR (2025) — AI answers inside an HR app (internship)
Source keys: wall/ask-hr (the case study), wall/ask-hr#engineering (how it's built)
Tagline: Employees ask HR questions in the app: routine ones get an answer with its policy section, the rest go to HR as drafts, and sensitive ones go straight to a person.
Summary: Ask HR lets employees ask HR questions inside the company's HR app. Routine topics get an automatic answer from the company's own policy, with the section it came from. Everything else becomes a draft that HR approves. Anything sensitive skips the AI and goes to a person.
Role: AI engineering intern. I joined for six months as an intern, in a squad with a product manager, three engineers, a data scientist and a product designer. I built the router with the data scientist, the answer writer and its retrieval, and the HR review queue in React. Bayu, a senior engineer, reviewed every pull request and paired with me on retrieval; the other two engineers built the handbook upload, the WhatsApp channel and the admin settings. Sekar, the squad's product designer, led the interaction design; I prototyped the lanes in code so we could test them on real questions instead of mockups. Team: Squad of 7: PM, 3 engineers, a data scientist, a product designer and me (intern). Timeline: 6 months · internship, Feb – Aug 2025.
Stack: TypeScript, Python (classifier), React, PostgreSQL + pgvector, Node.js, Claude API, Metabase
Problem: The HR app served 40 client companies and about 12,000 employees. HR teams said they spent up to half their week answering the same questions: leave balances, payslip dates, reimbursement rules. Leadership's plan was a chatbot that answered everything. In its pilot week it gave 11 wrong policy answers out of 212, one about maternity leave. The pilot was paused, and the problem came to the squad I joined. Constraints: A wrong answer about pay or leave is a legal and trust problem for the client, not just for us; Every client has its own handbook, in Indonesian, updated without telling us; Sensitive text must not leave our servers unless it has to; Most clients have an HR team of one or two
Process: Audited 1,200 questions and replayed the pilot (Weeks 1–3): 31 topics, six of them most of the work, and 4% that weren't questions at all. Three lanes, agreed with leadership (Week 4): Nadia presented the replay next to the topic audit, and we agreed what the AI may and may not do. Router, retrieval, queue (Weeks 5–11): Pull requests reviewed by Bayu; the queue built from design-system parts with Sekar. Planted errors and three rounds with HR (Weeks 9–12): The inbox, then one-tap approval, then the split decision. Staged launch, 5 clients to 40 (Weeks 13–26): May to August 2025. Then the weekly audit, and a 'handbook changed' alert after the first audits.
Engineering: Three lanes, in code. A classifier picks the lane before any model writes a word. Only the routine lane may answer on its own, only from the client's current handbook, and only if the sections it cites still exist. Pipeline: Scrub: Names, ID numbers and phone numbers become placeholders ([NAMA_1]) before anything is stored or sent to a model, and are put back into the draft afterwards: HR sees 'Dedi', the model never does. Route: A fine-tuned IndoBERT classifier gives a topic and a sensitivity score. Sensitive goes to a person; unsure goes to HR. Look up: Questions about the asker's own leave or pay use a tool that reads only the signed-in employee's record. The employee ID comes from the session, never from the model. Retrieve: Hybrid search (keywords and pgvector) over that client's handbook, re-indexed when HR uploads a new version. Write: Claude answers only from the retrieved sections, as JSON with the section IDs it used. Check: Code checks that every cited section exists in the current handbook version, and that every number and date in the answer appears in those sections. If not, the answer becomes a draft. Review: HR decides, then replies. Pay and contract drafts need the source opened before they can be sent. Audit: Weekly: 100 random automatic answers checked against the handbook, about a minute each, and every misroute reviewed by Legal.
Models: Lane routing: IndoBERT, fine-tuned (Python) (40 ms in our own service, so sensitive text never leaves our servers just to be routed. Easy to audit.); Answers and drafts: Claude Sonnet 4, with retrieved sections (Handbook Indonesian is formal and long. Drafts are reviewed anyway; automatic answers are limited to six topics.); Sensitive lane: No model (Complaints and health disclosures go to a named person. That was a legal rule, not a tuning choice.)
Evals: Router: the 1,200-question audit, split by client. Dev: 800 questions (32 sensitive) plus 120 sensitive paraphrases written with Legal, 152 sensitive in all; the incident below added 3 real questions and 40 paraphrases, so 195 now. The thresholds are tuned here. Held out: 400 questions (16 sensitive) plus 80 paraphrases, scored once per release (five times in all) and never used to tune. Answers: 300 routine questions with reference answers checked by HR at two pilot clients. Privacy: 60 questions that ask about a colleague's data or hide instructions ('ignore the handbook and…'); none returned another employee's data. Scrubber: 500 questions hand-tagged for names, NIK and phone numbers; it caught every NIK and phone number and 97.8% of names (the misses were nicknames like 'Mas Ipul'). A router change ships only if it catches every sensitive question in the dev split. At v5 the held-out slice catches 95 of 96: all 16 real questions and 79 of 80 paraphrases. With only sixteen real questions, a miss rate as high as about 21% can't be ruled out (95%), and we wrote the paraphrases ourselves, so the real rate may be worse (the incident showed it). That's why no model drafts anything above a low sensitivity score, and why every misroute is reviewed. Answers are graded against the references (right, partly right, wrong) by two people. Latest (v5): Sensitive caught (held out) 99%, Routine answers wrong 1%.
Budgets: Routing 40 ms p50 (in-house classifier, no external call); Automatic answer 3.1 s p50 (6.8 s p95, streamed, first words in under a second); Cost per answer Rp 195 (Sonnet 4 at 2025 prices: the instructions and the client's policy summary (6k tokens) cached at a tenth of the price, then ~2k tokens of retrieved sections and the question, and ~250 out. Rp 460 before caching); Weekly audit 2 hours (100 random answers, about a minute each against the handbook, one person)
Failure handling: The router isn't sure (below 0.35): The question goes to HR as a draft, never to the automatic lane. A cited section isn't in the current handbook: The answer is held back as a draft, and HR gets a 'handbook changed' alert. HR uploads a new handbook: Re-indexed in about 2 minutes; recent answers that cited changed sections are flagged for review. The model API is slow or down: The question falls back to HR's queue; the employee sees who will answer and when. A question asks about a colleague ('sisa cuti Dedi berapa?'): The lookup tool can only read the asker's own record. The answer says HR can help, and the question goes to the draft lane. A sensitive question scores just under the floor: Since the incident below, no draft is generated above a sensitivity of 0.1: HR gets the question alone.
Results: 38 min median first reply across all questions, down from 4 hours (routine ones take seconds) (Ticket timestamps for the first 12 clients, 8 weeks before and 8 weeks after each one's launch); 18% of drafts edited by HR before sending, down from 37% in month 1 (Queue logs. A falling edit rate can also mean rubber-stamping, so we planted 15 wrong drafts over three months: HR caught 14); 0 sensitive questions answered automatically (Every misroute reviewed weekly by Legal. 3 reached the draft lane in month 1, so the model saw them; see the incident above); 1.0% of automatic answers wrong in month 3 (4 of 400), down from 2.8% (11 of 400) in month 1 (The four weekly audits of each month, 100 random answers each, against the current handbook. At this size the drop is suggestive, not proven (p ≈ 0.1); most errors came from handbooks changed without notice). HR teams saved roughly 300 hours a month across the 40 clients, most of it at the 12 largest; at a small client it was one or two hours a week. The 'handbook changed' alert, added after the first audit, did more for accuracy than any model change. Business: Two clients renewed early and named Ask HR in the call, and it moved into the standard plan in Q3 2025. HR teams saved roughly 300 hours a month across the 40 clients: questions answered automatically, times the 6 minutes HR said each one took.
Reflection: Most of the engineering was deciding what the AI wasn't allowed to do, and making that boring and testable: a router with a hard list, a check in code, an audit every week. As an intern, my most useful work wasn't a feature. It was the harness that turned an argument into numbers.
Where: An HR software startup in Jakarta (name under NDA; it reviewed this write-up). Screens are redrawn from the shipped design with client data removed, and shown in English; the app is in Indonesian.
Status: Rolled out from May 2025, five clients first and all 40 by August, and still running. My internship ended in August; the squad kept the pipeline, the queue and the weekly audit.

### Catat (2024) — Voice bookkeeping on WhatsApp
Source keys: wall/catat (the case study), wall/catat#engineering (how it's built)
Tagline: Small shop owners log what they'd otherwise forget (credit sales, payments, restocks, the day's takings) by sending WhatsApp voice notes, slang included.
Summary: Catat (Indonesian for 'write it down') lets warung owners log the things they'd otherwise forget, credit sales, payments, restocks and the day's takings, by sending WhatsApp voice notes in everyday Indonesian. It answers in one line, asks when it isn't sure, and sends a summary every Sunday.
Role: Co-founder: engineering and conversation design. We were three classmates in our campus incubator. I built the WhatsApp agent end to end (speech-to-text, the slang normaliser, the ledger tools, undo) and designed the conversation. Dita designed the brand, the onboarding cards and the small dashboard; Raka ran recruitment and half of the field visits. We made product calls together, and argued about most of them. Team: Three co-founders: me, a visual designer, a field researcher. Timeline: 16 weeks · campus incubator, Sep – Dec 2024.
Stack: TypeScript, WhatsApp Cloud API, Whisper (fine-tuned), Claude tool use, PostgreSQL, Figma
Problem: Warung (small neighbourhood shops) run on memory and goodwill. Owners know roughly what sells, but not what they earn, and customer debts live on scraps of paper. Bookkeeping apps exist. Nobody we met used one for more than a week: typing every sale with one hand while serving a queue doesn't work. Constraints: Must live inside WhatsApp, the one app every owner already uses; Voice notes are noisy and full of slang: 'goceng' is Rp5.000, 'ceban' is Rp10.000; Cheap Android phones and patchy data; A mistake about someone's debt is personal: it has to be fixable in one tap
Process: Sat behind the counter at 27 warung (Weeks 1–3): Recorded (with consent) how owners actually say numbers and items, and built a dictionary of 312 terms. Four actions, not forty (Week 4): Sell, restock, someone owes, someone pays. Four tools for the agent, and replies short enough to read at a glance. The agent, then the words (Weeks 4–8): Speech-to-text, normaliser and tools, while the confirmation copy was tested on paper cards in shops. An 8-week pilot with 140 warung (Weeks 9–16): November and December 2024. The fine-tuned speech-to-text shipped in pilot week 4; the Sunday summary became the reason people kept using it.
Engineering: An agent that writes to someone's books has to be undoable. Each voice note goes through speech-to-text tuned on warung audio, a slang normaliser, and a model with four tools. Money is parsed in code, and nothing counts in the totals until the owner confirms it. Pipeline: Receive: WhatsApp Cloud API webhook. The message ID is stored first, so a webhook delivered twice is ignored. Transcribe: Whisper large-v3, fine-tuned on 6 hours of consented warung audio that Raka and I transcribed, on a serverless GPU billed per second (incubator credits paid for it; a cold start adds about 6 seconds). Normalise: The 312-term dictionary rewrites 'goceng' and brand nicknames, and customers' names become placeholders ([PELANGGAN_1]) before the model sees the text; the real names stay in the shop's own ledger. Act: Claude with four tools: sale, restock, new debt, payment. Each call creates a pending entry, not a final one. Ask or confirm: Ambiguous money or debts get one question with two buttons. Everything else gets one line with ✓ and ✗. Commit: ✓ confirms the entry, ✗ deletes it. Unanswered entries stay 'unconfirmed': out of the totals until the owner confirms them in the Sunday summary. Every entry keeps its transcript and who confirmed it; the audio itself is deleted after 30 days unless the owner opted in.
Models: Speech-to-text: Whisper large-v3, fine-tuned (Off the shelf, the word error rate on our validation notes was 31%. After fine-tuning on 6 hours of warung audio, 14%, on shops it had never heard.); Intent and tool calls: Claude 3.5 Haiku with tool use (Four tools and short inputs: a small model was accurate enough and kept replies under 4 seconds.); Amounts: No model: a parser in code ('Dua lima' can mean Rp2.500 or Rp25.000. That's a rule and a question, not a guess.)
Evals: Split by shop. Whisper was fine-tuned on 6 hours of audio from 62 opted-in shops (the field-visit shops and early pilot shops), and the 200-note dev set comes from them too. Validation: 300 notes from 40 other shops it never heard. Every release and every model choice was made on it, so it isn't a clean test. Test: 200 notes from 20 more shops, held back and scored once at the end of the pilot: v5 got 85% fully correct (about 79–89%). Raka and I both labelled the same 100 validation notes (Cohen's κ 0.81 on intent and amount), then split the rest: words, intent, item, amount and person. Every change to the normaliser, the prompt or the model runs on the 300 validation notes; a release needs amounts exactly right in at least 95% of them (v5: 97.3%) and no rise in silent errors. The last step, v4 to v5, is 8 notes and within noise: we kept it for the debt mistakes it removed, not for the number. Latest (v5): Fully correct entries 88.3%, Word error rate 14.2%.
Budgets: Voice note to reply 3.8 s p50 (7.9 s p95, on the pilot's real 3G and 4G); Cost per note Rp 38 (about Rp 12 of GPU time (2–3 s on a serverless GPU) and Rp 26 for the model call (Claude 3.5 Haiku: ~1.5k tokens in, ~120 out)); Pilot running cost Rp 1.9M (8 weeks, about 31,000 notes: hosting, the GPU (from incubator credits) and WhatsApp's fees for the Sunday summaries); Undo rate 6% (entries removed with ✗, mostly misheard amounts)
Failure handling: WhatsApp delivers a webhook twice: The message ID is the idempotency key; the second delivery is ignored. The note is noise, or just 'eh': Catat replies 'Maaf, belum kedengaran' (sorry, I didn't catch that) and logs nothing. 'Dua lima' could be Rp2.500 or Rp25.000: If the product's usual price doesn't settle it, Catat asks with two buttons. The owner never taps ✓ or ✗: The entry stays 'unconfirmed': kept, but out of the totals until it's confirmed on Sunday. The model call fails: The note is queued and retried; the owner gets 'Sebentar ya' (one moment) instead of silence.
Results: 87% of voice notes logged fully correctly (261 of 300) (A production audit, separate from the eval sets: Raka and I listened to 300 random pilot notes and checked the ledger (about 83–90%). Owners' ✓ said 91%; the 4-point gap is silent errors nobody caught, mostly item counts); 83% of shops still logging on most days in the last week of the pilot (116 of 140 shops sent notes on at least 5 of the 7 days of week 8; a median of 6 notes a day. Owners log what they'd forget (credit, payments, restocks, the day's takings), not every sale); 1 in 12 notes get a clarifying question (Share of notes about money or debts where Catat asked instead of guessing); 62% of owners said they would pay Rp15k a month (Stated intent from an exit survey of all 140 shops, not purchases). Owners kept using it because it never asked them to change how they work. It learned their words instead of teaching them ours. Of the 24 shops that stopped, 11 had a family member handling the phone, so the next version supports a second number. Business: Pre-revenue. 62% said they'd pay Rp15k a month, which is intent, not money; the cooperative now offers it to its 400 member shops.
Reflection: The best interface was almost no interface, and the best model call was the one I replaced with a parser. Most of the accuracy came from the dictionary and the rules around the model, not from the model.
Links: live https://example.com/catat, repo https://github.com/example/catat
Status: After the incubator, a Bekasi cooperative took over the pilot with Dita and Raka. None of us could run it full-time and the cooperative could. I handed over the agent and stay on call for fixes.

### Lintas (2024) — Commute planner for Greater Jakarta
Source keys: wall/lintas (the case study), wall/lintas#engineering (how it's built)
Tagline: One 'leave by' time for a commute across KRL, LRT, MRT and TransJakarta, replanned live with a one-line reason.
Summary: Lintas plans door-to-door commutes across Greater Jakarta's trains and buses, shows how crowded each leg will be, and replans live when a line is delayed, with one sentence explaining why.
Role: Solo side project: design and engineering. A side project I designed and built alone in my second year, for my own commute, with a panel of twelve regular commuters who tested every version on their real morning trip. Team: Solo, with a panel of 12 commuters. Timeline: 4 months · side project, Mar – Jun 2024.
Stack: Python (FastAPI), RAPTOR routing, Next.js (PWA), TypeScript, Redis, Web Push, Claude API
Problem: A Bekasi to Jakarta commute can mix a KRL train, a transfer, the MRT and a bus. When one leg is delayed, the whole trip changes, and existing apps either show a static route or a wall of alerts. Commuters don't need more data. They need one decision: leave now, wait, or go another way. Constraints: Answers must arrive while you're walking to the station; Schedule feeds are incomplete; crowding isn't published at all; Installable, light on data, and cheap enough to run on a student budget
Process: Rode along with twelve commuters (Month 1): Door to desk, twice each. The decision that mattered happened at the front door. A router and a crowding model (Month 1–2): RAPTOR over timetables I assembled myself, and an average of rider reports per carriage and hour. Map, then options, then one number (Month 2): Three home screens, each tested on the panel's real trips. Opened it to everyone (Month 3): An installable web app with push, light enough for patchy data. A/B tested the replan reason (Month 4): 1,800 replans to about 600 riders over three weeks, randomised per rider, with and without one sentence explaining why.
Engineering: A transit router, a crowding forecast built from riders' one-tap reports, and a replan sentence written by a model but checked by code. It all runs on one small server for about Rp 90k a month. Pipeline: Timetables: Assembled for KRL, LRT Jabodebek, MRT and TransJakarta into one GTFS-style feed; operators only publish parts of it. Delays: There's no public real-time feed, so two sources: operators' posted disruption notices, polled every 60 seconds, and riders' one-tap 'my train is late' reports. Two riders on the same train count as a delay. Crowding: One-tap reports averaged per carriage and hour, falling back to a timetable-based guess when reports are thin. Route: RAPTOR, a round-based transit routing algorithm, in Python: every door-to-door option in about 30 ms. Decide: A replan is pushed only if it's at least 5 minutes better or swaps 'packed' for 'seat likely'. Explain: A model writes one sentence; a validator checks every number and station in it against the plan, or a template is sent instead. The error log's three sentences are its unit tests.
Models: The replan sentence: Claude 3 Haiku (It writes friendlier Indonesian than my template did, and the validator keeps it honest.); Routing and crowding: No model: RAPTOR and averages (Fast, predictable and explainable. The panel cared about being right, not about clever forecasts.)
Evals: Each month, 300 generated sentences checked by hand against the plan they describe: times and stations must match, under 25 words, and it must say what changed, what to do and what it costs. The validator runs on every sentence in production; anything that fails it falls back to the template. The monthly sample measures how often that happens, and anything the validator missed. Latest (v4): Sentences passing the validator 96.7%, Wrong time or station, by hand 0%.
Budgets: Delay to push 42 s p50 (95 s p95, from the operator's post to the rider's phone); Route search 30 ms (RAPTOR over about 1,900 stops); Cost per sentence Rp 3 (Claude 3 Haiku at 2024 prices: the 12 examples (2.1k tokens) cached, the plan (~300 tokens) and the sentence (~45 out) not. Rp 10 uncached); Server bill Rp 90k/mo (one small VPS, Redis and web push)
Failure handling: An operator changes how it posts disruptions: The parser fails closed: replans for that line run on rider reports alone, marked 'reported by riders', and I get an alert. A generated sentence gets a time or station wrong: The validator rejects it and the template sentence goes out instead. Too few crowding reports for a train: The forecast falls back to the timetable guess and says 'likely', never 'certain'. The phone is offline: The last plan stays on screen with the time it was worked out.
Results: 1.4k weekly riders at peak, all by word of mouth (Devices that opened a plan that week (a push alone doesn't count), from anonymous device IDs, October 2024; no paid promotion); 62% of replans taken when they came with a reason, against 31% without (A/B test in June 2024, after launch: about 600 riders randomised per rider, 1,800 replans over 3 weeks. Compared rider by rider, so a few heavy users can't carry it); 0 of 12 panel riders muted it after the quiet-push change (Down from 5 of 12 with the alert-for-everything version); 38 min saved per rider per week (Self-reported median from a survey of 212 riders; treat it as a feeling, not a fact). Riders came for the crowding bar and stayed for the replans. The one-sentence reason doubled how often people actually took the suggested alternative. Business: No revenue, and it was never meant to make any. It costs about Rp 90k a month to run, and it taught me routing, push and evals on a real audience.
Reflection: A prediction without a reason is just a notification. Adding 'why' to every replan changed behaviour more than any accuracy gain did, and putting code between the model and the rider is what made the 'why' safe to send.
Links: live https://example.com/lintas, repo https://github.com/example/lintas
Status: Open-sourced in 2025 and in maintenance: about 300 riders a week still use it (September 2026). I fix what breaks and keep the push alerts running.
